seoTitle: How to Get Your Webhook Signing Secret in Stripe Safely
metaDescription: Find and copy your Stripe Webhook Signing Secret to verify payment events securely. This guide covers creating an endpoint and protecting the secret.
intro: Stripe webhooks let your app receive real-time updates on payments, subscriptions, and refunds, but none of that works until you've created a webhook endpoint and grabbed its Signing Secret. That secret is what proves an incoming request actually came from Stripe rather than someone spoofing your endpoint, so skipping it isn't really an option for anything handling real payments. This guide covers exactly where the webhook tools live in the Stripe dashboard, how the endpoint-creation wizard works, and what to do with the secret once you have it.

steps.heading: Understand why the Webhook Secret matters
steps.body: Every webhook event Stripe sends to your endpoint is signed using this secret. Your app recomputes that signature on its end and compares it against the one in the request header — if they match, the event genuinely came from Stripe; if not, it's rejected. Without this check, anyone who knows your endpoint URL could send fake payment or subscription events and your app would have no way to tell the difference.

steps.heading: Find Webhooks in your Stripe dashboard
steps.body: From the dashboard's Overview screen, the left-hand Shortcuts panel under Workbench lists Overview, Webhooks, Events, Logs, and More, with a separate Documentation section below it for API reference, SDKs, and Developer settings. Webhooks sits right alongside Events and Logs because they're related — Events is the full history of things happening in your account, while Webhooks is where you configure which of those events get pushed out to your app automatically. If you're working in a sandbox, a banner across the top confirms you're testing rather than touching live data, which is the safer place to build this out first.

image.caption: The Stripe dashboard overview, with Webhooks listed in the Shortcuts panel alongside Overview, Events, and Logs.

steps.heading: Start creating an event destination and choose your events
steps.body: Clicking to create a new webhook opens a three-step wizard, starting with Select events. Events are grouped by category — Billing, Capability, Cash Balance, Charge, Checkout, Climate, Coupon, Credit Note, and more — each showing how many distinct event types fall under it. Only select what your app actually needs to react to; a checkout flow generally cares about Checkout and Charge events, while a subscription business will also want most of Billing. Selecting fewer, more targeted events keeps your endpoint's logic simpler and reduces the traffic it has to filter through.

image.caption: Step one of the event destination wizard, with event categories like Billing, Charge, Checkout, and Coupon listed alongside their event counts.

steps.heading: Choose Webhook endpoint as your destination type
steps.body: Step two asks where Stripe should send these events: a Webhook endpoint (a URL you host that receives the events directly) or Amazon EventBridge (routes events into your AWS account instead). For most standard integrations — a Node, Python, or Ruby backend receiving and processing Stripe events — Webhook endpoint is the right choice. EventBridge is really only relevant if your infrastructure is already built around AWS event routing.

image.caption: Step two of the wizard: choosing between a Webhook endpoint you host yourself and routing events through Amazon EventBridge.

steps.heading: Enter your endpoint URL and finish creation
steps.body: The final step asks for the actual URL your app exposes to receive these events — something like https://yourapp.com/api/stripe/webhook — along with an optional description to help you tell endpoints apart later if you create more than one. Once you confirm, Stripe generates the endpoint and, critically, a unique Signing Secret tied specifically to it. Each endpoint you create gets its own separate secret, so if you're running both a test and a live endpoint, expect two different values.

steps.heading: Copy the secret and store it safely
steps.body: The Signing Secret appears on the endpoint's detail page, usually hidden behind a reveal or copy action rather than shown in plain text by default — a small friction that's intentional, since anyone with this value can forge valid-looking webhook events. Copy it into your app's environment variables (a .env file locally, or your host's secret manager in production), never directly into source code. Keep it out of version control entirely, and if it's ever exposed accidentally, roll it by deleting the endpoint and recreating it rather than trying to patch around the leak.

faq.question: Where do I find my Webhook Signing Secret in Stripe?
faq.answer: It's shown on the details page of the specific webhook endpoint you created, reachable from the Webhooks shortcut in your Stripe dashboard's left-hand panel.

faq.question: Is the Webhook Secret the same as my Stripe API key?
faq.answer: No. The Webhook Signing Secret verifies that incoming webhook events genuinely came from Stripe, while your Publishable and Secret API keys are used to make outbound calls to Stripe's API — they're separate credentials with separate purposes.

faq.question: What happens if I don't use the Webhook Secret to verify events?
faq.answer: Without verification, your endpoint has no way to confirm that an incoming request is genuinely from Stripe, which leaves it open to spoofed payloads pretending to be real payment or subscription events.

faq.question: Can I have a different Webhook Secret for each endpoint?
faq.answer: Yes — every webhook endpoint you create through the event destination wizard gets its own unique Signing Secret, even if two endpoints point to the same app.

faq.question: Should I choose a webhook endpoint or Amazon EventBridge?
faq.answer: A webhook endpoint is the right choice for most integrations, where your own app receives and processes the events directly. EventBridge only makes sense if your infrastructure is already built around routing events through AWS.
